question: An analyst has forty Claude-drafted product descriptions. About half will be posted on the public website and half will sit in an internal catalogue, and she has time to check roughly twenty of them properly before the deadline. What should she do first?
options: A) Check the longest descriptions first, because a longer description contains more claims to get wrong.
B) Check the descriptions in the order they were generated, until the time she has set aside runs out.
C) Sort the batch by where each description will end up and how hard an error there would be to undo.
D) Ask Claude to mark the descriptions it is least sure of, and check only the ones that it flags.
correct_answers: C) Sort the batch by where each description will end up and how hard an error there would be to undo.
explanations: Length is not a proxy for stakes. A short line of public-facing copy can be far more damaging than a long internal entry, so sorting by length would leave the riskiest items unchecked.

Working in generation order spends her limited review time at random. The website copy and the internal catalogue do not carry the same consequences, so order of arrival is the wrong basis for choosing.

Correct. With review capacity smaller than the batch, the first step is to triage by exposure and reversibility. Externally published copy that is hard to retract earns the scarce review time; an internal entry anyone can correct does not.
A model's own stated uncertainty is a weak and unvalidated signal, and it says nothing about consequences. It can be a useful supplement, but it cannot decide which outputs need human eyes.
